title: Ethical AI design
desc: Design an AI feature with fairness, privacy and safety in mind
content_html:
What We're Doing

Ethics is what guides responsible innovation — deciding not just what an AI can do, but what it should do. Not everything that is possible to build should be built. In this lesson we take a real AI product idea and pressure-test it against fairness, privacy and safety, then redesign it to be something we would be proud to ship.

You'll Need

  • A whiteboard or paper
  • One or two "product idea" scenario cards (a face-scanning school gate, a homework-grading bot, a friend-recommending app)

Step-by-Step Activity

  1. As a group, agree on a short list of values an AI you build should uphold — for example fairness, privacy, safety, and being explainable.
  2. Pick one product idea card and read it aloud.
  3. Pressure-test it against your values: Who could it treat unfairly? What personal data does it collect, and where is that stored? How would someone appeal a wrong decision?
  4. Redesign the idea to fix the biggest problems you found — change the data it uses, add a human check, or drop a risky feature entirely.
  5. Each group presents a 60-second "ethics review" of their before-and-after design.

Examples

  • A grading bot that has never seen essays from English-as-a-second-language students may mark them unfairly.
  • A school gate that stores every child's face needs to answer: who can see that data, and for how long?
  • A recommender that only ever shows more of the same can trap someone in a narrow bubble.

Facilitation Tips

  • There is rarely one "right" answer — reward well-argued trade-offs over tidy conclusions.
  • Keep bringing it back to real people: "who is affected, and could it harm them?"
  • Let groups disagree; ethical design is a negotiation, not a checklist.

Discussion Questions

  • What is the difference between what an AI can do and what it should do?
  • Why does being able to explain a decision matter so much for trust?
  • Who should be responsible when an AI makes an unfair decision — the coder, the company, or the user?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Write a three-point "code of conduct" for an AI your school might use.
  • Medium: Audit a real app you use and list one fairness, one privacy, and one safety question it raises.
  • Hard: Fully redesign a feature you think is unfair, and write a short memo defending your changes to its makers.
